text.p: There's much made of the presence of porn on the Internet, but try this exercise one day: Go to any Internet search engine and look for the word "sex." Then search for the word "money."
You'll learn what really titillates online.

In fact, a quick search on Yahoo!, one of the most well-known and well-stocked Web search tools, turned up five sites for "invest" for every two "sex" sites. And there's much under both headings that you wouldn't want small children to see.

With more than 5,000 easily identifiable investing sites on the World Wide Web, it's evident some of them are going to be abject ripoffs: money stealing schemes you've already been warned about aplenty by the state securities regulators, consumer groups and more.

But what about the vast majority of the sites, those that have legitimate commercial purpose but may or may not be useful? How can you use the Internet as an investing tool instead of letting it use you?

There are hundreds of really good Web sites that carry all the information a stock or mutual fund investor would ever want. How can you choose among them? And how can you use the abundance of information they carry for your own good? Follow these guidelines to avoid being whipsawed by the Web.

-- Before you commit your first click, decide what kind of investor you are. If you only want to select mutual funds, that eliminates a lot of sites there. If you are a buy-and-hold investor, you can ignore all of the fast-paced sites aimed at day traders.

If, on the other hand, you want to sit and your desk and buy and sell all day, you can skip the more staid how-much-you-need-to-save-for-retirement sites. Nailing down your own investment philosophy before you go online serves two purposes: It saves you time online and it gives you the backbone to resist some of the come-ons you'll encounter.

-- Find the sites you already own first. If you are happy with the funds you have and the broker you are using, check out their Web sites before you head to new ones. Chances are you'll find additional data that may help you manage your portfolio. The more forward fund companies and brokers let you access your account on line for balance checks and trades.

Even the slower-going ones will be doing this soon, so if you don't have access yet that's not a compelling reason to close all your accounts. If you don't know the addresses of your own funds, check your latest statement; it's probably there.

-- Go to the sites of the independent industry leaders. For mutual funds, Morningstar (www.morningstar.net) and Lipper (www.lipperweb.com) have been the leading researchers since the old fashioned paper and mail days. They're still leading online.

Stock investors already used to getting solid information from the American Association of Individual Investors can check them out at www.aaii.org. or get information straight from SEC filings at www.sec.gov. A decent free stock screening Web site can be found at www.stockmaster.com.

-- Check dates. There's a lot of "immediacy" online that's not as new as you think. Sure, just about everyone is updating quotes every 15 minutes, but once you start looking for earnings data, quarterly reports and more, you'll find some sites are behind the times.

-- Decide what information you really need and set a budget for paying for it. If you need real time quotes, you'll pay for it. If you need more than an occasional stock research report, you'll pay for it; either directly or through higher commissions with a more expensive broker.

Watch your online expenses: If you find yourself spending $15 a month (not counting basic Internet connect charges) for information to help you invest your $2,000 IRA contribution, that's a 9 percent return you'll have to make just to cover your research costs. That's okay, if you admit that what you have is not a research need, it's a hobby. Then you can call that $15 a recreational expense and not a cost of investing.
